summary:
NEBUS — Integrated Martian Terrain Assessment and Autonomous Surface Station

NEBUS is an integrated engineering concept designed to support future human exploration of Mars by combining terrain-aware astronaut safety with an autonomous surface monitoring station in Gale Crater.

Module 1: uses NASA planetary datasets, including MOLA/HRSC elevation models, MGS TES thermal inertia, Curiosity RAD radiation observations, and Mars Trek, to assess terrain conditions and identify potential safer routes for extravehicular activities (EVAs).

Module 2: introduces a six-legged autonomous station featuring multilayer radiation shielding, thermal insulation, and hybrid thermoelectric energy harvesting. The design was developed in Autodesk Fusion 360 and evaluated using SimScale structural simulations and Python-based thermal models.

Under defined engineering assumptions, the hybrid energy model estimates 19.98 Wh per Martian sol, compared with a target autonomous monitoring demand of 16.00 Wh/sol.
NEBUS demonstrates how NASA's open planetary data can be integrated with computational engineering to support safer, more energy-efficient, and potentially sustainable human operations on Mars.
details:
NEBUS is an integrated Martian engineering concept designed to support future human exploration by combining terrain-aware EVA route assessment with an autonomous surface monitoring station in Gale Crater.

Module 1 — Terrain & EVA Route Assessment

Using NASA Mars Trek, MOLA/HRSC elevation models, MGS TES thermal inertia data, and Curiosity RAD observations, we analyzed terrain slope, surface roughness, radiation conditions, and potential astronaut walking routes. Our analysis identified candidate routes using a slope threshold below 15°. NASA TES data yielded a thermal inertia of 405 SI at the proposed site.

Module 2 — Autonomous Surface Station

We developed a detailed, multilayer, six-legged autonomous surface station in Autodesk Fusion 360, integrating composite radiation shielding, thermal insulation, and thermoelectric interfaces. The CAD model underwent body consolidation during assembly optimization.

The protective dome incorporates fused silica, a melanin–graphene oxide–UHMWPE composite, and silica aerogel insulation. The landing legs feature Ti-6Al-4V structural components, boron-containing shielding layers, and ground-coupled thermoelectric interfaces.

SimScale dynamic structural analysis estimated a maximum Von Mises stress of 0.6324 MPa and a maximum displacement of 0.27 mm under the simulated conditions.

Using NASA REMS temperature observations as environmental references, we developed a hybrid energy model combining ground-coupled footpad TEG and dome UV-photothermal TEG. Under defined engineering assumptions, the model estimates 19.98 Wh per Martian sol against a target autonomous monitoring demand of 16.00 Wh/sol.

Innovation & Impact

Future Mars missions face interconnected challenges, including hazardous terrain, radiation exposure, extreme temperature variations, and limited energy availability. NEBUS was designed to address these challenges through a unified engineering approach.

Its key innovation lies in combining NASA-driven EVA route planning with a multifunctional autonomous surface station. Rather than relying on separate systems for radiation protection, thermal management, and energy harvesting, NEBUS explores how multilayer materials and hybrid thermoelectric technologies can perform complementary functions within a single structure.

By integrating planetary data analysis, structural simulation, and energy feasibility modeling, NEBUS aims to support safer astronaut mobility, more resilient surface infrastructure, and reduced dependence on external power for low-energy monitoring operations.
